chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: Operators manually pour a corrosive liquid from open pails and currently rely on splash goggles, face shields, and aprons. Which action best improves the control strategy?
options: Evaluate closed-transfer or pump-fed engineering controls first, then specify PPE for the residual splash risk.
Replace the current PPE with thicker garments and leave the open-transfer method unchanged.
Limit each operator to two pours per shift while keeping the same open containers and work method.
Require a signed PPE acknowledgment as the primary control before the next transfer begins.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: PPE is the last line of defense because it does not remove the hazard. Feasible elimination, substitution, or engineering controls should reduce the source or pathway first; PPE remains necessary for residual and upset risks.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Increasing PPE alone leaves the hazardous transfer method and its failure opportunities unchanged.
Exposure-time limits are administrative controls and do not control a sudden corrosive splash during a single pour.
Documentation supports a program but does not reduce the corrosive-liquid hazard or replace higher-order controls.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132 - General Requirements
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, hazard assessment and PPE limitations, pp. 385-388; OSHA 1910.132(d), hazard assessment and equipment selection

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A facility has completed a PPE hazard assessment for its machine shop. Which record best satisfies the OSHA certification requirement?
options: A purchasing list showing the brands and prices of PPE ordered for the machine shop.
A certification naming the workplace, certifier, assessment date, and identifying itself as the PPE hazard-assessment certification.
A monthly inspection checklist signed only by employees who wear PPE in the area.
A training roster that lists the hazards but does not identify who certified the workplace assessment.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA requires written certification of the workplace hazard assessment with the workplace identified, the person certifying it, the date or dates, and language identifying the document as the certification.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Purchasing information does not certify that the workplace hazards were assessed.
An employee inspection checklist can support implementation but is not the required hazard-assessment certification.
Training records do not replace the separate certification of the assessment and its responsible certifier.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132 - General Requirements
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, Hazard Assessment, pp. 385-388; OSHA 1910.132(d)(2)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.concept: Prescription eye protection and side protection
questions.stem: An employee who wears prescription glasses must grind metal parts that can eject fragments from the side. Which arrangement is appropriate?
options: Ordinary prescription glasses with no side shields because the lenses are impact resistant.
A face shield alone, provided it extends below the chin and is cleaned before the task.
Prescription safety eyewear with side protection, or compliant over-glasses that preserve both lens positions.
Tinted safety spectacles without prescription correction because the grinding task lasts less than fifteen minutes.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Eye protection must address the flying-object hazard, including side protection, while accommodating prescription lenses without disturbing the proper position of either the prescription or protective lenses.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Ordinary prescription eyewear is not automatically compliant impact protection and lacks the required side protection for flying objects.
A face shield is secondary protection for many hazards and does not by itself provide the required primary eye protection.
Task duration does not remove the need for both visual correction and protection appropriate to the hazard.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.133 - Eye and Face Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, eye and face protection, pp. 391-393; OSHA 1910.133(a)(2)-(3)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A technician opens a line that may release a pressurized corrosive splash. The procedure currently requires only a face shield. What is the best correction?
options: Keep the face shield alone because its larger surface provides complete eye protection.
Replace the face shield with ordinary safety spectacles because they seal more tightly around the eyes.
Use a darker welding lens in the face shield so the corrosive liquid cannot penetrate it.
Add chemical-splash goggles as primary protection and retain a compatible face shield for broader face coverage.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For severe splash exposure, goggles provide primary sealed eye protection and a face shield adds secondary coverage of the face. The combination addresses both the eye and face hazard.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A face shield can leave gaps and is generally used with, not instead of, primary eye protection for splash hazards.
Ordinary safety spectacles do not provide the sealed splash protection of chemical goggles.
Filter-lens shade controls optical radiation; it does not improve chemical-splash resistance.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 1910 Subpart I Appendix B - PPE Selection Guidelines
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, eye and face protection, pp. 391-393; OSHA Subpart I Appendix B, eye and face selection guidelines

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.concept: Head protection for impact and electrical hazards
questions.stem: Maintenance employees work below overhead material handling and near exposed conductors that could contact the head. What head-protection criterion is most important?
options: Choose a helmet rated for falling-object impact and the applicable electrical shock hazard.
Select any bump cap as long as the shell has no visible cracks and fits comfortably.
Use a metal hard-hat shell because it distributes electrical current around the head.
Choose head protection only for the more frequent hazard and manage the other hazard with warning signs.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The helmet must match all identified hazards. OSHA requires protective helmets for falling-object exposure and electrically protective helmets where exposed conductors could contact the head.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Bump caps do not provide the protection required for falling-object and electrical hazards.
Conductive metal head protection can increase electrical risk and is not the required electrically protective design.
PPE selection must address the credible combined hazards rather than ignoring one because it is less frequent.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.135 - Head Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, head protection, pp. 389-391; OSHA 1910.135(a)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A maintenance route exposes workers to dropped tools, sharp scrap that may pierce soles, and a residual electrical-shock hazard. Which footwear decision is best?
options: Issue conductive footwear because it provides the greatest protection from every electrical hazard.
Select compliant footwear with impact, puncture, and electrical protection matched to the assessed hazards.
Use ordinary leather work boots and add metatarsal guards only after an injury occurs.
Choose the lightest safety-toe shoe because toe protection automatically covers sole puncture and electrical hazards.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Footwear must be selected for the specific hazards identified. Different performance features address impact, compression, puncture, static discharge, and electric shock; one feature does not automatically cover the others.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Conductive footwear serves specialized static-control applications and can be inappropriate where electric-shock exposure exists.
Ordinary boots are not a substitute for hazard-matched protective footwear, and controls should be selected before an injury.
Safety-toe performance alone does not establish puncture resistance or electrical-hazard protection.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.136 - Foot Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, foot and leg protection, pp. 400-406; OSHA 1910.136(a)-(b)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A process changes from a dilute water-based cleaner to a concentrated solvent blend. What is the most defensible way to select replacement gloves?
options: Keep the existing gloves because all products marketed as chemical-resistant provide equivalent protection.
Choose the thickest glove available without considering the chemical or the task being performed.
Match glove material to the chemicals, contact duration, task demands, and manufacturer breakthrough data.
Select gloves by color code alone because manufacturers use universal colors for solvent compatibility.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: No glove protects against every hazard. Selection must be based on performance relative to the chemicals and the actual task, including duration, conditions, physical stress, and needed dexterity.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The phrase chemical-resistant is not a universal performance rating, and glove materials differ substantially by chemical.
Thickness alone does not establish compatibility, breakthrough time, usability, or protection against the specific mixture.
Glove colors are not a universal chemical-compatibility system and cannot replace performance data.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.138 - Hand Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, arm and hand protection, pp. 398-400; OSHA 1910.138(b)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: Which PPE payment policy is consistent with OSHA general-industry requirements?
options: Employees must pay for all required PPE because the equipment remains their personal property.
The employer must pay for ordinary weather clothing and every pair of non-specialty work boots used at the facility.
Employees may be charged for replacement PPE whenever normal wear makes the original equipment unusable.
The employer pays for required PPE except qualifying off-site non-specialty safety-toe footwear and items employees lose or intentionally damage.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA generally requires employer payment for required PPE but provides specific exceptions, including non-specialty safety-toe footwear permitted off the job. Replacement PPE is employer-paid except when lost or intentionally damaged by the employee.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Required PPE is generally provided at no cost; ownership does not create a blanket employee-payment rule.
Ordinary clothing and qualifying non-specialty footwear are among the specified payment exceptions.
Normal wear is not the same as loss or intentional damage and does not shift replacement cost to the employee.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.132 - General Requirements
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, PPE payment rule, p. 385; OSHA 1910.132(h)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A new employee has been assigned a tight-fitting half-mask respirator. Which step must occur before fit testing or required workplace use?
options: A medical evaluation must determine the employee’s ability to use the respirator.
The employee must complete one full shift in the respirator to demonstrate tolerance.
The supervisor must select a cartridge change date based on the employee’s ability to smell the contaminant.
The employee must purchase a personal facepiece so the employer does not influence the fit result.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Respirator use can impose a physiological burden. OSHA requires the employer to provide a medical evaluation before the employee is fit tested or required to use the respirator at work.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Requiring workplace use before medical clearance and fit testing reverses the required sequence and creates risk.
Cartridge service life is not a substitute for medical evaluation, and odor is not a reliable universal warning method.
The employer is responsible for the respiratory program and appropriate equipment; personal purchase does not replace the required evaluation.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, respiratory protection program, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(e)(1)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: An employee passed a fit test six months ago, but the company changes to a different make and model of tight-fitting facepiece. What is required before use?
options: Allow immediate use because the employee passed a fit test within the same calendar year.
Fit test the employee with the new facepiece before use and continue testing at least annually.
Perform only a user seal check because it replaces fit testing whenever the assigned protection factor is unchanged.
Delay testing until the employee reports leakage or discomfort during a hazardous task.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A different respirator facepiece requires a new fit test before use. OSHA also requires fit testing at least annually and when physical changes could affect fit.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A recent test on another facepiece does not establish fit for the newly selected make and model.
A user seal check is required each time the respirator is donned but does not replace formal fit testing.
Waiting for leakage during exposure is not an acceptable way to validate the fit of a new facepiece.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, fit testing definitions and program elements, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(f)(2)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: Entry testing at sea level shows an atmosphere containing 18.8% oxygen, with the contaminant concentration not yet characterized. Which respiratory decision is appropriate?
options: Use a half-mask air-purifying respirator because its cartridges remove the oxygen deficiency.
Use an N95 filtering facepiece because oxygen concentration is unrelated to respirator selection.
Treat it as oxygen-deficient and IDLH; use an approved positive-pressure atmosphere-supplying respirator for entry.
Permit entry without a respirator if a portable fan is operating near the opening.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA defines oxygen deficiency below 19.5% and generally treats oxygen-deficient atmospheres as IDLH. Air-purifying respirators do not supply oxygen; IDLH entry requires the specified positive-pressure SCBA or supplied-air configuration with auxiliary SCBA.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Air-purifying cartridges remove selected contaminants but cannot add oxygen to the atmosphere.
A particulate filter does not correct oxygen deficiency or address an uncharacterized IDLH atmosphere.
Ventilation may be part of control, but its presence alone does not demonstrate safe oxygen and contaminant conditions for entry.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, respirator types and limitations, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(b), (d)(2), and oxygen-deficiency definition

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A contaminant has an OSHA exposure limit of 2 ppm. A selected half-mask respirator has an assigned protection factor of 10, and the contaminant IDLH value is 30 ppm. What is the maximum use concentration based on these facts?
options: 2 ppm, because a respirator cannot be used above the exposure limit.
30 ppm, because the IDLH value always becomes the routine maximum use concentration.
200 ppm, because the exposure limit is multiplied by the APF twice for a half-mask respirator.
20 ppm, because APF × exposure limit equals 20 ppm, below the IDLH concentration.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: The calculated MUC is APF × exposure limit = 10 × 2 ppm = 20 ppm. Because 20 ppm is below the stated IDLH value and no lower cartridge limit is given, 20 ppm controls.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Respirators may be selected to control exposure above a limit when used within their assigned protection and other program requirements.
The IDLH value is a ceiling on routine MUC calculations, but it does not replace a lower APF-based result.
The APF is applied once; multiplying it twice overstates the respirator’s protective capability.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, assigned protection concepts, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(b) and 1910.134(d)(3)(i)(B)
questions.formula: MUC = APF × occupational exposure limit, limited by IDLH and cartridge/canister performance

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A gas cartridge has no NIOSH-certified end-of-service-life indicator, and workers cannot reliably smell the contaminant. How should the employer control cartridge replacement?
options: Use objective service-life data to establish and document a cartridge change schedule in the respiratory program.
Allow each worker to replace the cartridge only after detecting odor or throat irritation.
Replace every cartridge at the end of the calendar month regardless of use conditions or supporting data.
Continue using each cartridge until breathing resistance increases, because vapor cartridges fail by particle loading.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: When no appropriate ESLI exists, OSHA requires a change schedule supported by objective information or data so cartridges are changed before the end of service life, with the basis documented in the program.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Odor, taste, or irritation is not a dependable universal warning and may occur after harmful exposure.
A calendar rule without objective support may be either inadequate or unnecessarily conservative and does not satisfy the required basis.
Increased breathing resistance is mainly associated with particulate loading and is not a reliable indicator of gas or vapor sorbent exhaustion.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, respirator limitations and program procedures, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(d)(3)(iii)(B)(2)

questions.chapterTitle: Personal Protective Equipment and Respiratory Protection
questions.stem: A worker passed the annual fit test but later grows a beard that crosses the sealing surface of the tight-fitting respirator. What is the appropriate response?
options: Allow continued use because an annual fit-test pass remains valid until the next scheduled test.
Remove the seal interference or use a compliant respirator that does not rely on that facial seal.
Tighten the head straps beyond the manufacturer’s instructions and document the adjustment as a substitute for fit testing.
Apply petroleum jelly to the sealing surface before each shift to fill gaps created by facial hair.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA prohibits tight-fitting facepieces when facial hair lies between the sealing surface and the face or interferes with valve function. An annual fit test does not override a later condition that compromises the seal.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Fit can become unacceptable after the test; facial-hair interference must be addressed immediately.
Overtightening can distort the facepiece, cause discomfort, and is not an accepted correction for seal interference.
Applying unapproved substances can damage materials and does not create a compliant, reliable facepiece seal.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 - Respiratory Protection
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 14, respirator fit and limitations, pp. 396-398; OSHA 1910.134(g)(1)
